paper.title_en: A deep intrinsic decline of accretion activity in GRS 1915+105 during 2025
paper.abstract_en: The canonical microquasar GRS 1915+105 has undergone unprecedented multiwavelength changes since 2018. Hard-X-ray NuSTAR observations in November 2025 failed to detect it, reaching flux limits several orders of magnitude below historical X-ray levels. The non-detection could reflect enhanced obscuration, a sharp decline in accretion power, or a combination of the two. Hiding an intrinsically luminous source requires effectively complete coverage by Compton-thick material to limit residual direct or scattered components to <~10^{-4} of the nuclear power. Free-free absorption by an ionised cocoon could also explain the lack of a self-absorbed compact jet in deep radio imaging in mid-2026. However, such a cocoon would reradiate the absorbed power, contrary to faint infrared emission observed by SPHEREx from September 2025 onwards, and consistent with the donor star alone. The source's position in the infrared-X-ray plane also now matches the locus of quiescent black-hole binaries. Together, the X-ray, infrared, and radio constraints exclude any quasi-static, Compton-thick cocoon capable of hiding an otherwise luminous source, and favour an intrinsic quenching in 2025. We propose that strong outflows associated with repeated multiwavelength flaring during 2023-2025 depleted the inner accretion flow, reducing its power by at least two orders of magnitude (rising to >~4 dex if the nucleus is now unobscured), and indicating a likely return of GRS 1915+105 to quiescence after 33 years, notwithstanding any rebrightening episodes in the near future. With disc veiling now minimal, the donor star, binary orbit, and residual accretion can be probed directly for the first time.
